templates.pattern: A community has two species with [N1] and [N2] individuals respectively. The total number of individuals is [TOTAL]. Calculate the Simpson diversity index D = 1 − [(n₁(n₁−1) + n₂(n₂−1)) ÷ N(N−1)].
templates.explanation:
Simpson's D = 1 − [n₁(n₁−1) + n₂(n₂−1)] ÷ [N(N−1)]
= 1 − [([N1]×[N1-1]) + ([N2]×[N2-1])] ÷ [[TOTAL]×[TOTAL-1]]
= [RESULT]

D ranges from 0 (no diversity) to 1 (maximum diversity). Equal numbers of each species gives maximum D. A value near 1 indicates a highly diverse community.

templates.pattern: A population of [N] individuals records [B] births and [D] deaths in one year. Calculate the per capita population growth rate r per year.
templates.explanation:
Per capita growth rate r = (births − deaths) ÷ population size
= ([B] − [D]) ÷ [N]
= [B-D] ÷ [N]
= [RESULT] per year

A positive r means the population is growing. r = 0 means births equal deaths and population size is stable. r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and is central to all population growth models.

templates.pattern: A carbon pool holds [STOCK] Pg of carbon and receives [FLUX] Pg of carbon per year from the atmosphere. Calculate the mean residence time of carbon in this pool in years.
templates.explanation:
Mean residence time = carbon stock ÷ carbon flux
= [STOCK] ÷ [FLUX]
= [RESULT] years

Residence time describes how long carbon stays in a pool on average. Carbon in the atmosphere has a residence time of about 5 years. Soil organic carbon can reside for centuries. Deep ocean carbon may persist for thousands of years.

templates.pattern: A leaf litter sample has an initial mass of [INIT] g and after [TIME] years has a remaining mass of [REMAIN] g. Calculate the decomposition rate constant k per year.
templates.explanation:
Decomposition rate k = −ln(remaining/initial) ÷ time
= −ln([REMAIN]/[INIT]) ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] per year

Higher k values mean faster decomposition. Tropical forests decompose leaf litter in weeks while tundra litter may take decades. Temperature and moisture are the key controlling factors.

templates.pattern: A population is growing at [R]% per year. Calculate the approximate doubling time in years using the rule of 70.
templates.explanation:
Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate
= 70 ÷ [R]
= [RESULT] years

The rule of 70 is a quick approximation. At 2% growth a population doubles in 35 years. At 7% it doubles in 10 years. World population grew at about 2% per year in the 1960s.

templates.pattern: A bacterial population starts at [N0] cells and has a doubling time of [DT] minutes. Calculate the population size after [T] minutes.
templates.explanation:
Population = N₀ × 2^(t ÷ doubling time)
= [N0] × 2^([T] ÷ [DT])
= [N0] × 2^[T/DT]
= [RESULT]

Exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely — it is limited by resources. Real populations follow logistic growth as they approach carrying capacity.

templates.pattern: A forest ecosystem covers [AREA] hectares and releases [RATE] tonnes of carbon per hectare per year. Calculate the total carbon flux in tonnes per year.
templates.explanation:
Carbon flux = area × carbon flux rate
= [AREA] × [RATE]
= [RESULT] tonnes/year

Carbon flux measurements are essential for understanding the global carbon cycle and predicting climate change. Forests act as carbon sinks when NPP exceeds respiration.

templates.pattern: A soil sample from an area of [A] m² contains [C] kg of carbon. Calculate the soil carbon density in kg/m².
templates.explanation:
Soil carbon density = total carbon ÷ area
= [C] ÷ [A]
= [RESULT] kg/m²

Soils store about 3 times more carbon than the atmosphere. Peatlands have the highest soil carbon densities. Soil disturbance releases stored carbon contributing to climate change.

templates.pattern: An ecosystem has two trophic levels with efficiencies of [E1]% and [E2]% respectively. Calculate the overall ecological efficiency from the first to the third trophic level as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Overall efficiency = (E1 ÷ 100) × (E2 ÷ 100) × 100
= E1 × E2 ÷ 100
= [E1] × [E2] ÷ 100
= [RESULT]%

Efficiencies multiply through trophic levels. Two levels each at 10% efficiency gives only 1% overall efficiency. This is why food chains rarely exceed 4-5 links.

templates.pattern: An organism ingests [ING] kJ of energy, loses [RESP] kJ through respiration and [EXC] kJ through excretion. Calculate the secondary productivity in kJ.
templates.explanation:
Secondary productivity = ingested − respiration − excretion
= [ING] − [RESP] − [EXC]
= [RESULT] kJ

Secondary productivity represents energy stored as new biomass by consumers. It is always less than ingested energy because some is always lost to respiration and excretion.
